claims.text: A deep neural network potential should replace the EAM reference in thermodynamic integration for multicomponent high-entropy alloys near melting.
The neural network potential can be trained on a broad and diverse set of ab initio liquid configurations.
A DFT-trained deep neural network potential can describe both solid and liquid states of a high-entropy material.
The proposed deep neural network potential can serve as a thermodynamic-integration reference instead of an EAM potential.
The many-body flexibility of the neural network potential enables it to represent diverse liquid atomic configurations more accurately than EAM.
More accurate representation of liquid configurations improves reference–target phase-space overlap.
Training on a rich ab initio dataset enables the neural network to represent complex liquid-phase interactions better.
Improved representation of liquid interactions reduces mismatch along the thermodynamic-integration path.
Reduced thermodynamic-integration path mismatch improves free-energy accuracy.
The intervention may reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch by more than 50% relative to TOR-TILD EAM references.
The intervention should produce free energies closer to full ab initio results than TOR-TILD EAM references do.
TOR-TILD EAM references have insufficient phase-space overlap because they cannot represent the many configurations of an ab initio liquid.
The method applies to high-melting multicomponent high-entropy alloys, typically containing five or more metallic elements, at or near melting.
The method is expected to be effective only in the high-temperature regime near the melting point.
Performance for simpler or lower-melting systems remains unverified.
The success of the potential depends strongly on the quality and representativeness of the ab initio liquid-configuration dataset.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction of approximately 50% in path mismatch would falsify the hypothesis.
Significant disagreement with full ab initio thermodynamic-integration free energies would falsify the hypothesis.
